title: Kurseong and Mirik Food: Momos, Gundruk and Oranges
meta_description: What to eat in Kurseong, Mirik and the tea villages: momos, thukpa, dal-bhat, gundruk, kinema, chhurpi, sel roti, Sittong oranges and estate tea, with prices.
summary: Food in Kurseong and Mirik is Nepali hill cooking with Tibetan and Bengali touches: momos, thukpa, dal-bhat, gundruk, kinema, chhurpi and dalle chilli pickle, with sel roti at festivals. Homestay dinners are the best meals. Add Sittong oranges in winter and estate tea all year. Most meals cost ₹80–250.

sections.heading: What the middle hills eat
paras: The food of Kurseong, Mirik and the tea villages is, first of all, the food of the Nepali-speaking families who came to clear and pluck the gardens from the 1850s. A daily meal is rice, dal and a vegetable curry, with a sharp pickle on the side. Around that base sit the dishes of the neighbours: momos and thukpa from the Tibetan and Sherpa kitchens, which are now everyday street food all over the hills, and a Bengali streak in the towns, where visitors from Kolkata and the plains have shaped what restaurants serve.

The best food here is not in restaurants at all. It is the dinner at a village homestay in Sittong, Latpanchar, Chimney or the Makaibari estate, cooked on a gas ring or a wood stove from what the family grows: mustard greens, squash, beans, potatoes, radish and, in the right season, oranges and fern shoots. If you only eat in hotels, you will miss most of what is described below.

sections.heading: Momos, thukpa and quick bazaar food
paras: Momos are the default snack and light lunch. In Kurseong bazaar and around Mirik's lake you will find them steamed or fried, filled with cabbage and onion, chicken or pork, and served with a thin soup and a red chilli sauce. A plate of eight to ten costs about ₹80–150, with pork usually the most expensive. Thukpa, a noodle soup with vegetables or meat, is the cold-evening meal and costs ₹100–180 a bowl.

Chowmein, the Indian-Chinese stir-fried noodle, is everywhere, and so is Wai Wai, the Nepali instant noodle, which locals eat dry from the packet as a snack or cooked as a soup. Small stalls near the Kurseong station and the Mirik jeep stand sell aloo dum, a spicy potato curry eaten with puffed rice or bread, and samosas, chops and pakoras for a few rupees each. These are cheap, filling and made fresh in the morning; eat at stalls with a steady local queue.

sections.heading: Dal-bhat and the homestay table
paras: Dal-bhat is rice and lentil soup, and in a homestay it arrives with several companions: a vegetable curry, often iskus (chayote squash, which grows on vines over every fence in these hills), saag of mustard or spinach leaves, a pickle and, if you eat meat, chicken curry or eggs. Refills are expected. Breakfast is often puri or paratha with aloo, or bread, eggs and tea.

The pickles deserve their own note. Dalle khursani, the small round red chilli of the Darjeeling and Sikkim hills, is one of the hottest chillies you will meet, and a pickle made from it is on most tables; try a little first. Radish pickle, tomato chutney with timur (Sichuan pepper) and bamboo shoot pickle are also common. Ask your host what is in season and you may get ningro, the curled tips of a wild fern, fried with garlic, or a soup of sishnu, stinging nettle, which is soft and earthy once cooked.

sections.heading: Fermented foods: gundruk, kinema and chhurpi
paras: Fermentation is how hill families have always stored food through the monsoon and winter. Gundruk is made from mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves that are wilted, packed tight and left to ferment, then sun-dried; it is cooked into a sour soup that is especially good with rice on a cold night. Sinki is the same idea with radish root. Kinema is fermented soybean, sticky and strongly flavoured, cooked as a curry with onion, tomato and chilli. Neither looks impressive, but both are worth asking for.

Chhurpi is cheese made from buttermilk. Soft chhurpi is crumbly and mild, cooked with chilli and tomato into a relish or curry. Hard chhurpi is dried in blocks until it is almost stone, then sold in strings of small cubes that people chew for an hour or more; you will see it hanging in Kurseong and Mirik shops. Many families also make a millet beer called tongba or chhang for festivals and guests; it is a household drink, not a tourist product, so wait to be offered.

sections.heading: Festival food: sel roti and more
paras: During Dashain and Tihar, between late September and November, every Nepali household in the hills makes sel roti, a ring-shaped bread of ground rice batter, sweetened and deep-fried until crisp outside and soft inside. It is eaten with tea, with aloo dum or on its own, and handed to visitors during Tihar. Some bazaar stalls sell it year round for ₹15–30 a piece, but it is best fresh in a home during the festivals.

Christmas brings cakes to the church families of Sittong and Kurseong, and Losar at Bokar monastery in February or March comes with khapse, fried pastries, and butter tea. If you are invited into a home at any festival, accept the food offered; refusing everything can seem unfriendly, and a small helping is fine.

sections.heading: Tea, oranges and what to take home
paras: You are in one of the world's great tea districts, so drink the local tea properly at least once. Darjeeling tea is usually drunk without milk: first flush from March and April is light and floral, second flush from late May and June is fuller and has the muscatel note, and autumn flush in October and November is rounder and deeper. Makaibari, Castleton, Gopaldhara, Goomtee and other gardens sell through shops in Kurseong bazaar and Mirik; estate tasting sessions, where offered, cost about ₹200–500.

Roadside stalls make sweet milky tea with dust tea, which costs ₹10–30 a cup and is what everyone actually drinks during the day. In winter, the small sweet mandarins of Sittong and the warmer slopes below Mirik are sold by the roadside and in the bazaars from about mid-November to January, at ₹60–120 a kg in the orchards. Mirik is also a cardamom area. Good things to carry home are a packet of first or second flush tea with the garden name printed on it, a string of hard chhurpi and a jar of dalle chilli pickle, sealed well.

sections.heading: What food costs
paras: Prices are indicative for 2025–26 in the bazaars of Kurseong and Mirik. Village shops are cheaper but have less choice; lakeside places in Mirik charge a little more.

A few habits keep you well on a hill trip. Drink filtered or boiled water, which most homestays provide in a jug or flask, and refill one bottle instead of buying plastic. Eat momos and fried snacks hot from the pan rather than from a tray that has stood for hours. Tell your host about allergies on the first evening, because many dishes use mustard oil and some use peanuts or sesame in pickles.

faqs.q: What food is Kurseong famous for?
faqs.a: Kurseong eats like the rest of the Darjeeling hills: momos, thukpa, dal-bhat, aloo dum and dalle chilli pickle, with Darjeeling tea from the gardens around it. What makes a trip here special is homestay food in the tea villages, such as gundruk soup, kinema curry, iskus and mustard greens. Tea from Makaibari and Castleton is the thing most people take home.

faqs.q: Where can I eat cheaply in Mirik?
faqs.a: Small eateries in the bazaar near the jeep stand and around the lake serve momos for ₹80–150, chowmein and thukpa for ₹70–180, and dal-bhat or a thali for ₹150–250. Lakeside places charge a little more for the view. For the best value, stay in a homestay that includes dinner and breakfast and eat lunch at a bazaar stall.

faqs.q: What is gundruk and how is it eaten?
faqs.a: Gundruk is fermented and sun-dried leafy greens, usually mustard, radish or cauliflower leaves. Families make it in autumn and store it for the lean months. It is usually soaked and cooked into a sour soup with tomato, onion and chilli, eaten with rice. The taste is sharp and tangy. Ask for it at a homestay, where it is often part of dinner in winter.

faqs.q: Is food in Kurseong and Mirik very spicy?
faqs.a: Most dishes are moderately spiced, but the chilli pickles and sauces can be very hot. Dalle khursani, the round red chilli of these hills, is among the hottest you will find in India. Momo sauce and pickles are served on the side, so you can control how much you take. Tell your homestay host if you prefer milder food.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians eat well in Kurseong and Mirik?
faqs.a: Yes. Dal-bhat with vegetable curries, saag, iskus, gundruk soup, kinema, aloo dum, chhurpi relish and veg momos are all vegetarian, and most homestays cook a vegetarian dinner on request. Some families use eggs freely, so mention if you avoid them. Jain or no-onion meals are harder to find in the villages; ask when you book.

faqs.q: Where can I buy genuine Darjeeling tea in Kurseong?
faqs.a: Buy packets that carry the name of a specific garden, such as Makaibari, Castleton, Goomtee or Gopaldhara, from tea shops in Kurseong bazaar or Mirik, or from the estate itself where it has a shop. Expect about ₹300–1,500 for 100 g depending on flush and grade. Avoid loose tea sold simply as Darjeeling with no garden or flush named.

Sel roti is a ring-shaped bread made from ground rice batter, lightly sweetened and deep-fried. Nepali families make it in large batches for Dashain and Tihar, and offer it to guests with tea or aloo dum. It is crisp outside and soft inside. Some stalls sell it year round for about ₹15–30 a piece, but it is best fresh at festival time.

faqs.q: When can I buy oranges in Sittong?
faqs.a: Sittong's Darjeeling mandarins ripen from about mid-November and are sold through December into January, with the peak in December. Orchard prices are about ₹60–120 a kg. You can also buy them by the roadside on the way to Mirik and in the Kurseong and Siliguri markets. Ask your homestay if you can walk through an orchard during the harvest.

Chhurpi is a cheese made from buttermilk in the Himalayan hills. Soft chhurpi is crumbly and is cooked with chilli and tomato into a relish or curry. Hard chhurpi is dried until very firm and sold in strings of small cubes that people chew slowly, sometimes for an hour or more. It travels well and makes a good small gift to take home.
